summary.text: At \(n=67\), the distinct indices \(147\) and \(2055\) both give residue sums equal to \(67\): respectively \(1+3+3+3+19+19+19\) and \(1+3+7+7+7+7+7+7+7+7+7\). Thus there are at least two occurrences at \(67\), contradicting the claimed value of one.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k)
\]
be the sequence A049802. Thus A383327 is the multiplicity function
\[
a(n)=\#\{m:F(m)=n\}.
\]
For positive \(n\), the definition used here may equivalently count only indices \(m<2^{n+1}\), since that is a sufficient bound for every index at which \(F(m)=n\). In particular, for \(n=67\), the set whose cardinality defines \(a(67)\) is
\[
E_{67}=\left\{m<2^{68}:\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor\log_2m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k)=67\right\}.
\]
We will exhibit two distinct elements of this set.

First take \(m=147\). Since
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\). The seven remainders occurring in \(F(147)\) are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
k&2^k&147\bmod 2^k\\ \hline
1&2&1\\
2&4&3\\
3&8&3\\
4&16&3\\
5&32&19\\
6&64&19\\
7&128&19.
\end{array}
\]
These values can also be read directly from \(147=128+19=128+16+3\). For example, reduction modulo \(2,4,8,16\) gives respectively \(1,3,3,3\), while reduction modulo each of \(32,64,128\) leaves \(19\). Consequently,
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=10+57=67.
\]
Moreover, \(147<256=2^8<2^{68}\). Hence \(147\in E_{67}\).

Now take \(m=2055\). We have
\[
2055=2048+7=2^{11}+7
\]
and
\[
2^{11}=2048\le2055<4096=2^{12},
\]
so \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\). Modulo \(2\), the remainder is \(1\), and modulo \(4\), it is \(3\). For every \(k\) from \(3\) through \(11\), the number \(2^k\) divides \(2^{11}\), while \(0\le7<2^k\). Therefore
\[
2055\bmod 2^k=7\qquad(3\le k\le11).
\]
There are \(11-3+1=9\) such values of \(k\). It follows that
\[
F(2055)=1+3+\underbrace{7+\cdots+7}_{9\text{ terms}}
       =1+3+9\cdot7
       =4+63
       =67.
\]
Also, \(2055<4096=2^{12}<2^{68}\), so \(2055\in E_{67}\).

The two exhibited indices are distinct, since \(147\ne2055\). Thus the two-element set
\[
U=\{147,2055\}
\]
is a subset of \(E_{67}\). To spell out the only membership case split involved: if \(x\in U\), then either \(x=147\), in which case the first calculation gives \(x\in E_{67}\), or \(x=2055\), in which case the second calculation gives \(x\in E_{67}\). Hence
\[
2=\#U\le \#E_{67}=a(67).
\]
In particular, \(a(67)\ne1\).

Finally, \(67\) is one of the numbers in the conjecture's specified set
\[
\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
If the conjecture were true, applying it to this member would give \(a(67)=1\). But the two explicit occurrences above give \(a(67)\ge2\), which is incompatible with \(a(67)=1\). Therefore the assertion that \(a(n)=1\) for every \(n\) in the displayed set is false.
